title: Vesper and the Atlas
premise: In 1848, in a city trembling on the edge of insurrection, Ines Galloway works the type cases of her father's print shop, convinced that revolutions are ink for other people's newspapers. Then a wounded stranger leaves a baby at their door with a single instruction: forget my face, and print what I've paid for. The payment buys plates for an underground atlas mapping the regime's secret prisons, and the child is the daughter of a disappeared dissident. As soldiers close in and her father's loyalty wavers, Ines must choose between the invisible life she's built and the dangerous, named self the atlas demands. In the end, the shop burns, the atlas escapes in a thousand hidden copies, and Ines, carrying the child, becomes one of the names she once helped others forget.
about_author: Rosalind Thackeray is a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century print equipment in provincial museums. Her fiction is drawn from marginalia, seized pamphlets, and the unattributed hands that kept forbidden presses running.

chapters.title: The Smell of Hot Metal
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Establish the print shop, the father's failing eyesight, and the city's restless calm. Ines sorts type for a government almanac, priding herself on being unremarkable. Emotional beat: quiet complacency, the comfort of small, exact work while history gathers outside like weather.

chapters.title: A Bundle at the Door
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, night. A bloodied stranger leaves an infant and a sealed packet, whispering 'forget my face.' Ines hides both before her father wakes. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into reluctant responsibility; the first crack in her belief that she stands outside events.

chapters.title: What the Plates Show
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She develops the stranger's plates: hand-drawn maps of prisons and vanished persons, an atlas of the regime's hidden geography. Her father recognizes a name on it—an old friend, disappeared years ago. Emotional beat: awe curdling into dread as the work's purpose becomes clear.

chapters.title: The Compositor's Oath
chapters.summary: Father's POV. He confesses his past printing for the resistance and his betrayal of a cell under interrogation. He wants to destroy the plates; Ines refuses. Emotional beat: inheritance of guilt, the first open rupture between father and daughter over what a printer owes the truth.

chapters.title: Apprentices of the Night
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. She recruits two allies: Sabine, a bookbinder with smuggling routes, and Tomas, a runaway compositor. First pages printed in secret. Emotional beat: exhilaration and found-family warmth—the intoxicating discovery that invisibility can be a weapon.

chapters.title: The Inspector's Proof
chapters.summary: Inspector Vasseur's POV. A state censor with genuine convictions, he traces contraband type to the Galloway shop but hesitates, moved by a printed page listing his own brother among the disappeared. Emotional beat: the antagonist's conscience complicating the net closing around Ines.

chapters.title: Distribution
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The atlas goes out hidden in Bibles, ledgers, and wallpaper rolls; the city begins to murmur names. Sabine is nearly caught; the child falls ill. Emotional beat: rising stakes and the cost of the work—every copy sold is a risk multiplied.

chapters.title: The Betrayal of Small Debts
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Terrified after his brother's arrest, he trades the shop's location to Vasseur for clemency. Ines learns of it with hours to spare. Emotional beat: heartbreak and fury; the theme of identity sharpened—Tomas chooses survival over self.

chapters.title: The Last Impression
chapters.summary: Ines and her father's POV, alternating. Soldiers surround the shop; father stays to run one final, defiant edition as a diversion while Ines flees through cellars with the child and the master plates. The shop burns. Emotional beat: grief, sacrifice, and the father's redemption in ink.

chapters.title: Vesper and the Atlas
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, months later. The revolution has come and half-failed; the atlas circulates as legend. Ines, renamed, keeps a small press in another city, the child—Vesper—asleep above the type cases. Emotional beat: hard-won resolution; identity no longer hidden but chosen, and the work unfinished but alive.
